rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poor Muslims were excused from the charity prerequisite, and the amount was left open so the directive would not burden them.
rows.anchor: The indigent were exempted from this directive so that this should not become a burden for the poor among the Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The charity condition was meant to curb the hypocrites’ growing secret conversations, which arose from their greed and stinginess.
rows.anchor: secret conversation launched by the hypocrites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miserly hypocrites would avoid private meetings; if they paid, the spending purified them spiritually and inclined them away from mischief.
rows.anchor: their spending became a means of their spiritual purification

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sincere compliance brought worldly and afterlife success and cleansed hearts; the directive sought people’s salvation, not the Prophet’s comfort.
rows.anchor: it would become a means for their betterment and success both in this world and in the Hereafter, and a source of cleansing their hearts.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poor and indigent people could continue meeting the Prophet privately without the charity restriction.
rows.anchor: as before the poor and the indigent can continue to meet the Prophet (sws) in private for their conversation without any such restriction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later verse abrogated the preceding directive and was placed immediately after it so the two verses remained adjacent.
rows.anchor: so that the abrogated and abrogating verses are adjacent to one another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Enough time had to pass for the initial directive to fulfil its purpose by stopping the hypocrites’ secret-conversation mischief.
rows.anchor: the objective of the initial directive would have been fulfilled

rows.speaker: Some exegetical narratives
rows.claim: Some exegetical narratives say that the two verses were separated only by morning and evening.
rows.anchor: Some exegetical narratives show that the two verses were just separated by morning and evening.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adjacency does not establish that only a few hours separated the verses’ revelations.
rows.anchor: However, this cannot be the reason for saying that there is little or no difference between the time of revelation of the two verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an also places a later-revealed abrogating verse immediately after the abrogated one; Sūrah al-Muzzammil is a clear example.
rows.anchor: A very clear example of this exists in Sūrah al-Muzzammil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The restriction addressed a temporary mischief and was lifted after it was checked or people learned to abstain; that purpose could not be achieved in hours.
rows.anchor: This purpose cannot be achieved in a few hours.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording indicates secret meetings declined: hypocrites desisted from stinginess, while sincere Muslims were deterred by poverty and by recognizing God’s disapproval.
rows.anchor: the increasing tendency of speaking in private with the Prophet (sws) was curtailed after this directive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase indicates that people neither dared to speak privately with the Prophet nor paid charity for such meetings.
rows.anchor: neither did the people dare to talk in private with the Prophet (sws) nor did the event of paying charity for it arise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression means God accepted their repentance; Islahi infers that they first became worthy of acceptance by feeling ashamed.
rows.anchor: means “God accepted your repentance.” Obviously, this acceptance by God must have been after

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some hard-hearted people may have ignored the warning, the community generally felt ashamed; God values a good sentiment held by most, so the restriction was lifted.
rows.anchor: when a good sentiment is found in most individuals of a community, He values this attitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to pray, pay zakāh, and obey the Prophet cautions Muslims to prevent another crisis or an opening for Satan’s whispering.
rows.anchor: as a watchful measure Muslims must specially be diligent in the prayer, in paying zakāh and in obeying the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The abrogating and abrogated verses form a parenthetical passage; once it ends, the discourse returns to the hypocrites.
rows.anchor: As soon as they ended, the discourse once again returns to the discussion regarding the hypocrites.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites’ real alliance is with the Jews, Islam’s enemies; they befriend them and use false oaths to infiltrate among Muslims.
rows.anchor: they befriend them, and on the basis of their false oaths have infiltrated among the Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Love of worldly life is their underlying malady and has made them allies of Satan.
rows.anchor: Their real malady is love for this world because of which they have become accomplices of Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s inalterable decree is that He and His messengers prevail and Satan’s faction is defeated.
rows.anchor: it is the inalterable verdict of God that He and His messengers shall always prevail and the faction of Satan will be vanquished.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith cannot coexist with friendship toward religion’s enemies; true believers sever even close family ties and, as God’s faction, succeed.
rows.anchor: True believers are those who sever all ties with such people even if they are their close relatives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening question expresses astonishment at hypocrites befriending those under God’s wrath while swearing that they side with Muslims.
rows.anchor: This is an expression of wonder on these hypocrites; on the one hand, they are friends to those who have incurred the wrath of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are true allies of neither side: faith cannot coexist with friendship for God’s enemies, while self-interest would make them dissociate rather than endure an assault.
rows.anchor: If they are faced with trying circumstances, these hypocrites will never be ready to bear any assault and will only declare their dissociation like Satan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They know they serve only their interests and use false oaths to please both the Muslims and the Jews.
rows.anchor: they fully know that they are with no one except with their interests; however, by swearing false oaths they want to please both

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those described as having incurred God’s wrath are the Jews, alluded to as al-maghdūb ʿalayhim in al-Fātiḥah 1:7.
rows.anchor: refer to the Jews who are alluded to by the words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the hypocrites also befriended Meccan idolaters, the passage focuses on Jews, who had primarily reared and guided them as agents among Muslims.
rows.anchor: these hypocrites were primarily reared and guided by the Jews, and had infiltrated among the Muslims as their agents.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites may think their oath strategy cleverly satisfies both sides, but it is a perilous game for which God has prepared grievous punishment.
rows.anchor: this is not a wise policy they have adopted; it is a perilous game that they are playing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their punishment includes worldly punishment reserved for those hostile to God and His Messenger as well as punishment in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: They will encounter the punishment in this world reserved for the enemies of God and His Prophet (sws) besides the punishment of the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their fake oaths shield them from accountability and religion’s demands; they retreat from the path they professed and feign piety, but face humiliation.
rows.anchor: Whenever they are called to account on any of their mistakes, they make use of their fake oaths to assure others of their innocence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣadd can be transitive or intransitive; here Islahi reads it intransitively as their desisting from moving toward God.
rows.anchor: Here it is used in the latter sense implying that they have desisted from moving towards God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s yokes are their attachments to wealth, wives, and children, which sap courage to pursue religion and impede progress toward God.
rows.anchor: This verse refers to the yokes which have hampered their

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth and children cannot save them in the slightest from God’s punishment.
rows.anchor: their wealth and children will not be able to save them in the slightest of ways from the torment of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In min Allāh, the governing noun muḍāf is elided; the intended sense is min ʿadhāb Allāh, from God’s punishment.
rows.anchor: There is an ellipses of the governing noun ( muḍāf) in the expression:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At resurrection they will again resort to false oaths to exonerate themselves, as they do before Muslims now.
rows.anchor: On that day, they will swear oaths to exonerate themselves from blame the way they are today swearing oaths before the Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi cites al-Anʿām 6:23 as a parallel about the idolaters’ oaths, though this segment cuts off before he completes the comparison.
